passage:
Saturday: at the barber shop in Madurai, Madhav, ten, waited his turn with an old children's magazine. On the back page was his sign: 'You are kind, but sometimes shy. You notice things others miss.' He read it three times. How did they know? He tore the corner off carefully and put it in his pocket.
Monday: at recess he showed it to Shankar. 'This is exactly me. I noticed the new boy had no pencil, remember?' Shankar shrugged. 'Okay.' Madhav smoothed the paper flat on his knee like a certificate.
Wednesday: the class teacher asked for volunteers for the school play. Madhav kept his hand down. At home he told his mother, 'It's not my fault. The magazine says I'm sometimes shy.'

qa.q: Where did Madhav find the horoscope?
qa.a: He found it on the back page of an old children's magazine at the barber shop in Madurai.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when he first read his sign?
qa.a: He felt amazed and understood, wondering how they knew, which is why he tore the corner off to keep it.

qa.q: What could Madhav do the next time he reads a line like that?
qa.a: He could read the other signs too and see if the same words fit Shankar or his mother, before letting it decide whether to join the school play.

qa.q: How might Madhav's mother feel when he blames the magazine for not volunteering?
qa.a: She might be surprised and a little worried that a general magazine line is now stopping him from trying something new.

grounding: A ten-year-old boy is sure a general magazine horoscope describes him exactly and even uses it to explain not volunteering.

passage: Sunaina, you're reading me your horoscope as if it were a letter written only to you. Come, sit with your Nandini Nani. When I was nine, in Shimla, my aunt kept film magazines under her bed. I wasn't supposed to read them, but I found the stars page. Mine said, 'You have a gentle heart, though you are sometimes shy with strangers.' I nearly cried. That was me! I was shy with the milkman! I copied it onto a slip and kept it in my geometry box for two whole years. Every exam, I'd open the box and read it for luck. I never once read the other signs. I didn't think to. Why would I? It was mine. Now, beti, read me what the other eleven say, and let's see how many of them are gentle and shy.

qa.q: Where did Nandini Nani keep the horoscope she copied?
qa.a: She kept it on a slip in her geometry box for two whole years.

qa.q: Why did young Nandini nearly cry when she read the stars page?
qa.a: She felt deeply seen, sure the line about a gentle heart and shyness was written about her alone, even the shyness with the milkman.

qa.q: What does Nani suggest Sunaina do, and why is it a good step?
qa.a: Nani asks Sunaina to read the other eleven signs aloud, which will show whether the same kind of words would fit almost anyone.

qa.q: How might Sunaina feel after hearing Nani's story?
qa.a: Sunaina may feel a bit caught out but also amused, seeing that Nani once treasured a line just like hers.

grounding: A grandmother recalls being certain at nine that a magazine horoscope described her exactly, never checking whether it fit anyone else.

subtype: Online quiz result feels like being seen [Actor]
passage: In the auto on the way home from tuition in Bengaluru, Abhinav took a quiz on his phone: 'Which Mythical Creature Are You?' Twelve questions. Result: 'Phoenix. You've been through more than people know, and you always rise. Some people don't see your true strength.' He read it twice and felt something warm in his chest. That was exactly it. Nobody at school knew how hard Class 9 had been. He screenshotted it and posted it on his story with 'finally someone gets it'. At dinner he showed his father. 'This is what I'm like, Papa. It's scientific, they analyse your answers.' The next day Irfan messaged: 'lol I got phoenix too.' Abhinav typed, 'Different for me,' and didn't reply after that. He kept the screenshot as his lock screen.

qa.a: Phoenix: he'd been through more than people know, always rises, and some people don't see his true strength.

qa.a: He could have stopped to think about why the same result fit Irfan, instead of saying 'Different for me' and ignoring the clue.

qa.a: His father might feel unsure or worried, since a twelve-question quiz is now being used as proof of who his son is.

subtype: Online quiz result feels like being seen [Actor]
passage:
'Didi, look. Which Season Are You. I got Autumn.'
'Read it, Sumit.'
'Thoughtful, loyal, and quietly misunderstood by people around you.'
'Mm.'
'It's so me. That's literally me.'
'Loyal, okay. Quietly misunderstood?'
'Nobody in this house gets me, Urmila Didi. That's the point.'
'Beta, your dal is getting cold,' said Ma.
'Ma, listen. It says I'm thoughtful. You always say I'm careless.'
'You left the gas on yesterday.'
'That was once! See, misunderstood.'
Urmila took his phone and scrolled. 'What does Spring say?'
'Who cares about Spring.'
'Kind, loyal, and often misunderstood by those close to you.'
'That's different.'
'How?'
Sumit took the phone back. 'Just is.' He changed his profile picture to an orange leaf before finishing his dal.

qa.a: Sumit got Autumn.

qa.a: He wanted to feel understood at home, so 'quietly misunderstood' matched how he felt and made the general words seem exact.

qa.q: What turning point could Sumit have used when Urmila read out Spring?

subtype: Reading or prediction that seems to know them [Receiver]
passage: Saurabh, my boy, you're asking whether to trust the man at the temple gate. Let your Sonali Bua tell you what happened to me. I was nineteen, the first girl in our family with an engineering seat, in Pune. A week before I was to leave, a face reader stopped me outside the market. He looked at me kindly and said, 'You carry an old hurt you rarely mention.' Beta, I went cold. I thought of my father's shop fire, which I never spoke about. I trusted him at once. Then he said, 'Going far west this year brings loss.' Pune was west. I cried for two days and nearly gave up the seat. My mother finally asked, 'What hurt did he name?' He hadn't named anything. I had filled it in myself. I went to Pune. So by all means listen to him, Saurabh. Just notice what he doesn't say.

qa.q: What did the face reader say about going far west?
qa.a: He said, 'Going far west this year brings loss.'

qa.q: Why did Sonali Bua trust the face reader so quickly?
qa.a: His line about an old hurt made her think of her father's shop fire, so she felt deeply seen and trusted him at once.

qa.q: Which question changed Sonali Bua's decision, and what can Saurabh learn from it?
qa.a: Her mother asked what hurt he had named, and she realised he named nothing; Saurabh can check whether a reader says anything specific before letting it steer him.

qa.q: How might the mother in Sonali Bua's story have felt watching her daughter cry for two days?
qa.a: She was likely worried that a stranger's warm words were about to cost her daughter a hard-won seat, which is why she asked such a careful question.

grounding: An aunt tells her nephew how a reader's warm, general line made her feel seen at nineteen and nearly steered her to give up a college seat.

subtype: Reading or prediction that seems to know them [Receiver]
passage: The Delhi train was six hours late, and Kunal, twenty, sat on his backpack on the cold platform at Jhansi with his phone at eight percent. A man with a notebook and a shawl sat beside him and offered to read his face for free. 'You carry an old hurt you rarely mention,' he said softly. Kunal's throat tightened. He thought of his mother leaving when he was small, something he told no one. The man patted his knee. 'And the partnership you're planning will bring loss.' Kunal stared. He and his friend Samir were about to start a small wedding photography business. How did he know? Kunal used his last battery to text Samir: 'maybe we wait a year. bad feeling.' Samir replied, 'what? since when?' Kunal didn't answer. The man was already talking to the next passenger.

qa.q: Where was Kunal waiting for the delayed train?
qa.a: He sat on his backpack on the cold platform at Jhansi.

qa.q: What was Kunal feeling when the man mentioned an old hurt?
qa.a: His throat tightened; he felt seen and moved, because he thought of his mother leaving, something he told no one.

qa.q: At what point could Kunal have stopped the reading from steering him, and how?
qa.a: Before texting Samir, he could have asked himself whether the lines were specific at all, and seen the man move to the next passenger with the same routine.

qa.q: How might Samir feel receiving 'maybe we wait a year. bad feeling.'?
qa.a: Samir would likely be confused and hurt, since their plan suddenly changed with no reason Samir could understand.

grounding: A young man stranded on a platform feels seen by a stranger's general line and lets that trust steer him to delay a business plan with his friend.

passage:
Counsellor's note, Kashish, career guidance centre, Tuesday:
Avni, 25, came in half laughing. Over the weekend her friends had booked an 'aura reading' at a café. The reader told her, 'You are a creative soul held back by the people around you.' Avni said she enjoyed it and felt a little flattered. Then, she said, she asked the reader whether 'a practical soul held back by her own doubts' would fit too. The reader agreed it might. She also asked for one thing she could check, like when her promotion letter would come. The answer was 'when the energy shifts'. Avni told me the reading was a nice mirror for thinking about whether she wants more creative work. But she said she won't resign from her accounts job because of it. We made a plan to look at design courses she can try on weekends first.

qa.q: What did the reader tell Avni at the café?
qa.a: The reader told her, 'You are a creative soul held back by the people around you.'

qa.q: How did Avni feel about the reading, based on the note?
qa.a: She enjoyed it and felt a little flattered, but she was also clear-headed enough to test it rather than believe it.

qa.q: Which question helped Avni most, and how does it link to her job decision?
qa.a: Asking whether the opposite line would fit too showed the reading was vague, so she used it for reflection and planned weekend courses instead of resigning.

qa.q: How might Avni's friends see her questions to the reader?
qa.a: Her friends might find her questions funny or a bit of a spoilsport at first, but they may also see she could enjoy it without being led by it.

grounding: A counsellor records a young woman who tests a vague reading by asking if the opposite fits and whether anything is checkable, enjoying it as reflection without letting it decide her career.

passage:
Losar night, Darjeeling. Writing this by the heater.
Binita's aunt reads tea leaves every year, and tonight she held my cup up to the lamp. 'Tenzin, you work very hard but sometimes doubt yourself. A big decision is coming over water.' Everyone went 'ooh' because they all know about the Singapore offer.
I liked it, honestly. It felt warm. But I asked, 'Aunty, would "you're confident but sometimes lazy" fit me too?' She laughed and said, 'Also true!' Binita kicked me under the table.
Then I asked if the leaves could say anything I could check, like the salary or when they'll reply. 'Leaves don't do numbers,' she said. Fair.
So, notes to self: I do doubt myself. Worth thinking about. But the offer gets decided on the contract, the team and whether I want to be that far from Amala. Not a teacup.
Still, the butter tea was excellent.

qa.q: What did Binita's aunt say was coming over water?
qa.a: She said, 'A big decision is coming over water.'

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about the tea-leaf reading?
qa.a: Tenzin liked it and found it warm, and took the line about self-doubt as worth thinking about, while not treating it as a prediction.

qa.q: What will Tenzin base the Singapore decision on instead, and why is that wise?
qa.a: On the contract, the team and whether Tenzin wants to be that far from Amala, which are specific and checkable, unlike the leaves.

qa.q: How might Binita have felt when Tenzin asked the aunt about the opposite line?
qa.a: Binita may have been embarrassed that Tenzin was testing Binita's aunt at a family festival, which is why Binita kicked under the table.

grounding: In a same-day diary a young adult enjoys a tea-leaf reading, tests whether the opposite fits and asks for something checkable, and keeps the job decision on real facts.

subtype: Loves the lopsided thing they made [Actor]

This week each child shaped a small clay diya pot. Pooja's leans to one side and has a thumb-dent in the rim. Today her mother brought a shiny painted pot from the market for our Diwali corner. Pooja put hers right next to it and said, 'Mine is the best.' When a friend said the painted one was prettier, Pooja held hers against her chest. 'I made the dent.' I let her place hers in front. subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: Tenzin, you're sulking because Miss said your bridge model sags. Let your Nirmala Paati tell you about my periscope. I was eleven, in Coimbatore, and I spent four afternoons on it: cardboard, two mirrors from my mother's old compact, black paint inside. It was beautiful. At the science exhibition, our teacher looked through it and said, 'The top mirror is at the wrong angle, Nirmala. Tilt it and you'll see over the wall.' I said, 'It works fine!' She tried to show me. I took it from her hands. I felt she was saying I was stupid, not the mirror. I went home and cried. My brother tilted the mirror the next day while I was at school. It worked perfectly. I was angry for a week. So, kanna, is Miss talking about you, or about the bridge?

qa.q: What did the teacher say was wrong with Nirmala's periscope?
qa.a: She said the top mirror was at the wrong angle and needed tilting to see over the wall.

subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: The school bus broke down on the flyover, and Gopika reached the science fair with only twenty minutes before judging. 'One wire's loose at the back, Gopika. Tape it down and it'll work.' 'It works at home, Ma'am.' 'It isn't working now. Twenty minutes, quick.' Gopika felt her face go hot. 'You think I did it badly.' 'I think one wire is loose.' Gopika turned the board away. 'The judges will press other questions.' Ma'am left the roll of tape on the table. The first judge pressed question four. Gopika stared at the tape, wishing she had used it.

passage: The college fest's ticket website was due to open at six in the evening, and at noon it was crashing every few minutes. Indu, twenty-one and leading the student tech team, traced it to one place: Vaibhav's hand-written image uploader. He had spent two weeks on it. The standard library the rest of the site used could do the same job in ten lines. 'Let's swap it,' Indu said. Vaibhav didn't look up from his screen. 'I just need to fix one thing.' At two, he said the same. At three, he showed her how clever his resizing trick was, the one he'd worked out at midnight. Indu noticed he never said the uploader was better. Only that he'd built it. At four she said, 'We'll keep your code in a folder. Let's use the library for tonight.' He nodded slowly and closed the file.

qa.a: She realised he never said it was better, only that he'd built it, which suggested he valued it for the effort he'd spent.

passage: Uma, you asked old Jaya from the third floor how to handle Kiran and his home-made login code. Well. When I was twenty-two, I led my first team, three of us, at a small Chennai startup. Our quietest developer, Ravi, had written his own sorting routine for the billing system. Three weekends of work. The standard library already had one that was faster and tested by thousands of people. I suggested we switch. Ravi went pale. He didn't argue about speed. He talked about the weekends, and the clever part he'd figured out on a bus. That's when I noticed: he loved it for what it cost him, not for what it did. I didn't win by arguing. I asked him to run both on a big file and time them. His took four minutes, the library's took six seconds. He was quiet for a while. Then he said, 'Okay. But can I keep mine?' Of course, I said.

qa.q: How long did Ravi's sorting routine take on the big file?
qa.a: His took four minutes, while the library's took six seconds.

qa.q: What did Jaya realise when Ravi talked about his weekends?
qa.a: Jaya realised Ravi loved the routine for what it cost him, not for what it did, since he never argued about speed.

qa.q: What could Uma try with Kiran, based on this story?
qa.a: Uma could ask Kiran to compare his login code with the standard library on a real test, rather than arguing, and let him keep his version.

qa.q: How might Ravi have felt when the timings came in?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed and quiet at first, but asking to keep his version shows he could accept the result while still valuing his work.

grounding: A senior engineer tells a young lead how, at twenty-two, they noticed a developer clinging to a hand-written routine because of the effort spent, not how well it worked.

passage:
'Trisha Di, it's lovely.'
'It's lopsided, Deepika. Look at the left sleeve.'
'I don't mind the sleeve.'
'Four months I sewed this blouse. Every evening after work.' Trisha held it up to the window. 'I keep wanting to say it's perfect.'
'So say it.'
'Let me ask myself properly. If I were starting today, for your wedding day, what would I choose?'
'And?'
'The boutique one. It fits. You'll be standing on stage for five hours.'
Deepika, the bride, looked at the hand-sewn blouse. 'Then I'm wearing yours at the mehendi.'
'You don't have to.'
'I want to. Every stitch is you.'
Trisha laughed and wiped her eyes. 'Fine. The boutique one for the wedding. Mine for the mehendi. And I'm not fixing that sleeve.'
'Good. It's my favourite part.'

qa.q: How long did Trisha spend sewing the blouse?
qa.a: Four months, every evening after work.

qa.a: She asked what she would choose if starting today for the wedding day, and picked the boutique blouse for the wedding while keeping hers for the mehendi.

qa.a: Deepika treasures it because every stitch is her sister, and even loves the lopsided sleeve as her favourite part.

passage: Last summer I spent six weeks making flashcards for my Class 2 reading group: two hundred of them, hand-lettered, with little drawings of mangoes and buses. I'm Indu, and I'd just started teaching at a school in Jaipur. Then in August the school bought a printed set. Clear fonts, sturdy card, pictures a child could read from the back row. My first feeling was annoyance. Mine were better, I told myself, because I'd made them. That night I asked myself a simpler question: if I were starting fresh today, which set would I choose for thirty children? The printed ones. My letters were uneven and some drawings were confusing. It stung. But I didn't throw mine away. They went to the reading corner, where children pick them up for fun, and I gave a bundle to Payal next door for her Class 1. She uses the mango one every day.

qa.q: How many flashcards did Indu make?
qa.a: Indu made two hundred flashcards, hand-lettered, with little drawings of mangoes and buses.

qa.q: What was Indu's first feeling when the printed set arrived?
qa.a: Indu felt annoyed and wanted to believe the hand-made cards were better just because of the work put into them.

qa.q: Which question helped Indu decide, and how did Indu still honour the hand-made cards?
qa.a: Asking which set to choose if starting fresh today led Indu to the printed ones for class, while the hand-made cards went to the reading corner and to Payal.

passage: Kamal, you left your crossword half done and now you can't sleep? Ha. Your Rukmini Paati knows that feeling. When I was nine, my father brought me a wooden tangram set from Madras. Seven pieces, and a card with a swan to make. I had the neck and the body, only the tail left, when Amma called me to fetch water from the well. All the way there and back, pot on my hip, I was turning triangles in my head. I spilled half the water hurrying. The moment I put the pot down, I ran to the veranda and fitted the last piece. A swan! That same morning I'd drawn a big kolam at the door. When Amma praised it that evening, I couldn't even remember what pattern I'd made. Finished things fly away, kanna. Unfinished ones sit on your shoulder.

qa.q: What shape was young Rukmini making with the tangram?
qa.a: She was making a swan, with only the tail left.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel while she fetched water?
qa.a: She felt restless and impatient to finish the swan's tail, turning triangles in her head so much that she spilled half the water hurrying.

qa.a: Kamal could jot down where the crossword stopped or finish one clue before bed, so the open task stops tugging.

qa.a: Amma might have been amused or puzzled that her daughter forgot a big kolam from that same morning but remembered every tangram piece.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at nine, a half-finished tangram kept pulling at her mind until she rushed back, while a finished kolam slipped from memory.

passage: Lokesh was four squares from finishing the number puzzle in his comic when the bus reached his stop. His brother Shankar tugged his sleeve. 'Get down, it's pouring!' They ran through the rain to the ration shop, where Amma had sent them for rice. The queue was long and loud. Lokesh stood holding the cloth bag, counting rows in his head. Seven in the corner, so the middle had to be... Shankar poked him. 'It's our turn, wake up!' Lokesh had forgotten to give the ration card. On the walk home, dripping, he kept muttering numbers. At home he didn't change his wet shirt. He opened the comic on the floor and filled the last four squares. 'Done!' Shankar held up yesterday's maze page. 'You finished this one too, remember?' Lokesh looked at it blankly. He didn't remember it at all.

qa.q: Where did Amma send Lokesh and Shankar?
qa.a: Amma sent them to the ration shop for rice.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh forget to give the ration card?

qa.q: What small step could Lokesh take next time he has to stop a puzzle suddenly?
qa.a: He could mark or quickly note where he stopped, so his mind can let go and focus on the errand.

qa.q: How might Shankar have felt about Lokesh during the errand?
qa.a: Shankar was probably a little annoyed, having to poke him and handle the queue while Lokesh muttered numbers.

grounding: On a rainy errand a boy can't stop thinking about his unfinished number puzzle and rushes to complete it, while a finished maze slips from his memory.

passage:
Thursday: Himani promised Pallavi, her cousin, that she'd watch just one episode of the dubbed drama before bed. It ended with the train doors closing between the two leads, one of them shouting a name the other couldn't hear. Black screen. Himani lay awake till one, running the scene backwards. What was the name?
Friday: in maths, she drew train doors in the margin and missed the homework instructions. Pallavi texted, 'did you watch 7?' Himani replied, 'NO. I'm being good.' That night she told herself she'd watch the first five minutes of episode seven, just to find out. Episode seven ended with a letter burning in a sink.
Saturday: she overslept badminton practice. Pallavi came over and found her with the laptop warm on her knees. 'You said one!' Himani groaned. 'It keeps stopping at the worst place. It's not fair.'

qa.q: How did the first episode end?
qa.a: It ended with the train doors closing between the two leads, one of them shouting a name the other couldn't hear.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling on Saturday when she said 'It's not fair'?
qa.a: She felt frustrated and a bit annoyed at the show, and at herself, because each ending pulled her into another episode.

qa.q: What choice could Himani make before starting the next episode?
qa.a: She could stop partway through an episode instead of at the end, or ask Pallavi to hold the laptop, so she isn't left with an open question at bedtime.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel finding Himani with the warm laptop?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel amused and a little worried, since Himani promised one episode and has now missed badminton practice.

grounding: Over three days a teenage girl keeps getting pulled into more episodes by cliffhangers, losing sleep and practice because the open question won't let her stop.

passage: Vishal, you're angry that the show stopped on a cliffhanger, and now you have to wait for season two? Please. Your Rajni Maasi waited a whole week, every week. I was fourteen, in 1991, and there was one family serial on Sunday mornings. The episode ended with the elder brother lifting a gun. Then music, and the title card. A week! I was so angry I threw my slipper at the television. Our set didn't even have a repeat. All week, in Hindi class, in the bus, washing plates, I was guessing: would he shoot? At whom? I asked Mrs Bhalla downstairs, who had a VCR, if she'd recorded it, just to watch the ending again for clues. The next Sunday I was sitting in front of the TV at eight, an hour early. And it ended on another cliffhanger. You're lucky, beta. At least you can stop yourself. Can you?

qa.q: How did the Sunday serial episode end?
qa.a: It ended with the elder brother lifting a gun, then music and the title card.

qa.q: How did Rajni Maasi feel when the episode ended on the cliffhanger?
qa.a: She was so angry that she threw her slipper at the television, and couldn't stop guessing all week.

qa.q: What choice could Vishal make, now that shows can be stopped any time?
qa.a: Vishal could decide to stop mid-episode or at a set time, instead of letting the open ending pull him into watching more.

qa.q: How might Mrs Bhalla have seen young Rajni asking about the recording?
qa.a: Mrs Bhalla might have found it funny and sweet that a fourteen-year-old was so desperate for clues that she came asking downstairs.

grounding: An aunt tells Vishal how, at fourteen, a weekly serial's cliffhanger kept her mind stuck all week and pulled her back an hour early.
